name: Utah

notes: Food and food ingredients are taxed at 3.0% everywhere (1.75% state, 1.0% local option, 0.25% county option); since January 1, 2026, food heated or made to order at convenience stores, gas stations and grocery stores is taxed as prepared food.

Alcohol is taxed at the general rate (plus the 1% restaurant tax on drinks served). Liquor, wine and heavy beer are sold through state stores at an 88.5% markup, and beer pays $13.85 a barrel; left out here.

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the general rate, on top of excise taxes left out here: $2.20 a pack of cigarettes, and 71% of the manufacturer's price on e-cigarettes from July 1, 2026 (86% on most other tobacco; moist snuff $1.83 an ounce).
Barber and beauty services aren't taxed.
Laundry and dry cleaning are taxed; self-service laundry isn't.
Gasoline and diesel are exempt from the sales tax and pay 37.9 cents a gallon from January 1, 2026 (indexed each January); left out here.

Restaurant food and drinks pay an extra 1% restaurant tax, levied by every county (Utah Code 59-12-603; the Tax Commission's simplified chart gives every area a restaurant rate 1% above its combined rate), which is counted in the restaurant rates here.
Diapers and menstrual products are taxed (their 2019 exemption was repealed in 2020).
Hotel stays pay the sales tax plus state, county and city lodging taxes (15.52% in all in Salt Lake City, 16.42% in Moab, 14.62% in Park City); not counted here.
Resort communities taxes (1.1% to 1.6% in Park City, Alta, Moab, Springdale, unincorporated Summit County and other resort towns) are part of the local rates here. Utah has no sales tax holiday.
Services below are from Utah Code 59-12-103 and 104.
gaps: Food for home is taxed at 3% everywhere in Utah: the state's 1.75% plus 1.25% local (the Tax Commission's chart).

Unincorporated Summit County pays 8.75% (its 1.1% resort communities tax since April 1, 2026) and the Snyderville Basin Transit District 9.05%; the rate files code both, and Erda and Lake Point (6.9%), with codes that aren't Census places, so their rates are set here from the Tax Commission's October 1, 2026 chart. Lincoln, in Tooele County, also pays 6.9%; it isn't a 2024 Census place, so its tracts take Tooele County's rate.

Codes in the rate files for the Inland Port, the Military Installation Development Authority's project areas and housing and transit reinvestment zones aren't places and are left out; their rates are those of the city or county around them except in the MIDA areas (8.35% to 10.05%).

Local sales tax propositions on the November 3, 2026 ballot, by the county clerks' unofficial counts: approved in Blanding (a renewal), Virgin, Washington City, Perry (repealing its transit tax), Salem and San Juan County; rejected in Santa Clara. None can take effect before April 1, 2027; each is noted on its page, not counted.

4906370: Blanding's voters reauthorized its 0.1% recreation, arts and parks tax (Proposition 2) on November 3, 2026, 114 for and 35 against (county clerk's unofficial count, state election results site).
4959390: Perry's voters approved repealing its 0.30% public transit tax (Proposition 6) on November 3, 2026, 1,333 for and 401 against (county clerk's unofficial count, state election results site); the repeal can take effect April 1, 2027 at the earliest, and the current rate is used here.
4967660: Santa Clara's voters rejected an emergency services sales tax of up to 1.0% (Proposition 3) on November 3, 2026, 805 for and 827 against (county clerk's unofficial count, state election results site; a 22-vote margin, so the canvass could change it).
4980530: Virgin's voters approved raising its resort communities tax by 0.5% (Proposition 4) on November 3, 2026, 130 for and 75 against (county clerk's unofficial count, state election results site); it can start April 1, 2027 at the earliest and isn't counted here.
4981960: Washington City's voters approved raising its emergency services sales tax by 0.67%, to 1.0% (Proposition 5), on November 3, 2026, 4,651 for and 2,715 against (county clerk's unofficial count, state election results site); the increase can start April 1, 2027 at the earliest and isn't counted here.
4965770: Salem's voters approved a 0.1% recreation, arts and parks tax (Proposition 8) on November 3, 2026, 1,634 for and 619 against (county clerk's unofficial count, state election results site); it can start April 1, 2027 at the earliest and isn't counted here.
49005: Unincorporated Cache County pays 7.25% inside the Cache Valley Transit District and 7.0% outside it (Tax Commission chart, October 1, 2026); 7.0% is used here, and 7.25% is the top of the range shown.
49037: San Juan County's voters approved a 1.0% emergency medical services sales tax (Proposition 7) on November 3, 2026, 564 for and 366 against (county clerk's unofficial count, state election results site); it can start April 1, 2027 at the earliest and isn't counted here.
49043: Unincorporated Summit County pays 8.75%, including its 1.1% resort communities tax (since April 1, 2026), and 9.05% in the Snyderville Basin Transit District, whose tracts take that rate here; Coalville, Francis, Henefer, Kamas and Oakley pay 7.65% (Tax Commission chart, October 1, 2026). Each of those towns holds less than half of the residents of every tract it is in: its own rate is used on its own page, and in a selection of whole tracts counts for the share of its tract's store jobs located in the town (its residents' share where the tract has none), the county's for the rest.

programs: Tax increment areas come from Salt Lake County's map of active project areas (those past their last tax year left out) and, elsewhere, from the 2025 tax entities the Tax Commission lists (via UGRC), which give no end dates, so an area whose last increment year was 2025 may still show. Housing and transit reinvestment zones are shown only where the 2025 tax entities list them (Vineyard Station and North Station); the zones on the Tax Commission's sales tax map (Salt Lake City, Sandy, South Salt Lake, South Jordan, Salt Lake Central, Kimball and Vineyard) and the Governor's Office of Economic Opportunity's Lehi, Farmington and Sandy Cairns zones aren't mapped. The Inland Port and the Military Installation Development Authority's project areas aren't shown. Utah Main Street's 29 communities (among them Logan, Cedar City, Heber City, Helper, Ogden, Price, Tooele and Vernal) have no map.

warn.text: Duchesne County's flag as a visitor economy rests on homes the Census counts as seasonal (1,449 of 9,028, 16.1%), mostly cabins in the Uinta Mountains that may be weekend places rather than tourism; it has 11 lodging places (0.5 per 1,000 residents), so read that flag with care.

Emery County's flag as a visitor economy rests on its 22 lodging places (2.2 per 1,000 residents), most of them motels in Green River on Interstate 70, which serve travelers as well as visitors to the San Rafael Swell, so read that flag with care.

Sanpete County's flag as a visitor economy rests on homes the Census counts as seasonal (1,059 of 10,578, 10.0%), largely mountain cabins, just over the cutoff; it has 21 lodging places (0.7 per 1,000 residents), so read that flag with care.

Beaver's page is built from the census tract that holds most of it; that tract's flag as a visitor economy rests partly on its motels along Interstate 15 (19 lodging places, 4.4 per 1,000 residents) serving travelers passing through, as well as cabins in the mountains, so read that flag with care.

Cedar City draws many visitors (the Utah Shakespeare Festival and nearby parks), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (2.9%) and its 35 lodging places (1.0 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs over the city as a whole, though one of its 7 census tracts is flagged on its own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Heber City draws many visitors (the Heber Valley Railroad and its resorts near Park City), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (3.2%) and its 11 lodging places (0.6 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Hurricane draws many visitors (Sand Hollow and the road to Zion), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (4.9%) and its 20 lodging places (0.9 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

St. George draws many visitors (Zion and the red-rock parks, golf and winter residents), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (9.87%, just under the cutoff) and its 83 lodging places (0.8 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs over the city as a whole, though 9 of its 17 census tracts, and Washington County as a whole, are flagged. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Salina's page is built from the census tract that holds most of it; that tract's flag as a visitor economy rests on homes the Census counts as seasonal (258 of 2,010, 12.8%), which may be hunting or weekend cabins rather than tourism, so read that flag with care.
